name: Hana Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a crew lead and the apprentice trainer at the river town depot, so I split my week between running jobs and teaching. On a job day we might be rebuilding a stretch of line along the river road, replacing old copper with new aluminium conductor, or putting in a new transformer for a school. On a training day I'm in the yard with four apprentices and the practice poles, watching them climb and tie in, and correcting how they hold the hot stick. I'm also on the storm team, so twice a year I get sent to another region for a week or two after a big storm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing an apprentice go from scared of the pole to running up it, because I remember being that scared girl myself. What wears me out is the storm trips, sleeping in a school gym with forty other lineworkers and working sixteen-hour days. My husband Dev is a pharmacist, so he works long hours too, and we're hoping to start a family next year. My parents ran a corner shop for twenty years, so I grew up knowing that work is work and you don't complain about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, the lines still need fixing, so back to work. At the depot nobody would be very surprised. I might share a funny post in the family group chat, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things go on as planned, which is good. Dev and I keep saving, we try for a baby next year, and I keep training apprentices. I'd be happy with that life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. We've got about four months saved and we'd keep putting a bit away for when I go on maternity leave. I'd maybe use the AI chat a bit more for writing up apprentice reports, because Dev showed me how and it does save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dev showed you the AI. How did that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He was using it to check drug interactions and I was laughing at him, then I tried it on a training plan and it gave me a decent first draft. I still rewrote half of it, because it didn't know that our practice poles are on a slope. But I use it now, once a week or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would maternity leave be a worry in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but the company's good about it, and my mum is ten minutes away and already talking about babysitting. The bigger worry is who trains the apprentices while I'm off. I'd want to pick that person myself.

S0.say: I'd say the lines still need fixing, so back to work, and nobody at the depot would be very surprised. I might share a funny post in the family group chat, but that's about it.
S0.think: It means things go on as planned, which is good: Dev and I keep saving, try for a baby next year and I keep training apprentices. I'd be happy with that life.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is, with about four months saved and more going aside for maternity leave. Uses the AI chat a bit more for apprentice reports, as Dev showed her.
S0.quote: I still rewrote half of it, because it didn't know that our practice poles are on a slope.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is grounded, family-centred and proud of training apprentices. She came to AI through her husband and uses it occasionally, with healthy scepticism. Her main concerns in this picture are family planning and handing over her apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good people adapt, and we'll be fine if we keep training properly. At the depot I'd tell the apprentices to learn the new tools but never forget the basics. I wouldn't make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one's alright for me. My job's mostly hands-on and partly teaching, and both of those still need a person for a while. If anything, the company would need someone to teach the crews how to use the new tools, and I'm already the trainer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of crews had tried the new tools, I'd learn them properly and build them into the apprentice training. I'd keep saving and we'd still try for the baby. Maybe I'd ask the company about a proper training role, more teaching and less storm work, which would suit a young family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit curious, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents ran a corner shop. Did they go through something like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the big supermarket opened on the edge of town, half the little shops closed in two years. My dad started opening later and stocking things the supermarket didn't, like spices and fresh bread from the bakery down the road. He used to say, the shop that sits and complains is the shop that closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of my apprentices, Luca, he's twenty and he's brilliant on the pole but can barely read a manual. If the job becomes more screens, I'd worry he gets left behind. I'd spend extra time with him, the way someone did with me.

S1.say: I'd say good people adapt and we'll be fine if we keep training properly. I'd tell the apprentices to learn the new tools but never forget the basics, and I wouldn't make a fuss online.
S1.think: This one's alright for me, because my job is hands-on and teaching, which both still need a person. The company would need someone to teach crews the new tools, and I'm already the trainer.
S1.do: Learns the new tools once a couple of crews have tried them and builds them into apprentice training. Keeps saving, still tries for the baby, and asks the company about a full training role with less storm work.
S1.quote: He used to say, the shop that sits and complains is the shop that closes.
S1.fieldNote: Her father's corner shop is her model for change: adapt, don't complain. She sees a natural path into training on new tools. Her concern for Luca, who struggles with reading, shows a mentor's eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to look after each other, families, churches and neighbours, because the government won't be ready. At the depot I'd say keep doing good work while there's work to do. I'd tell people not to panic, even if I was worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's frightening, because it's not just my job, it's Dev's too. A pharmacy is the kind of place AI would take over quickly. We'd both be at risk right when we wanted to start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put off trying for a baby by a year or so, which would be very hard. We'd save everything we can, cutting back on the trip to see Dev's family abroad, and get our four months up as high as we can. I'd ask the company to put me on training crews for the robots, because they'd need someone to show them where the dangers are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Scared, but I'd still feel I had my family around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said putting off the baby would be very hard. Can you tell me more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've been planning it for two years. My mum has already bought a little blanket, which I told her was too early. Telling her we're waiting because of robots would feel ridiculous, and also not ridiculous at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell people not to panic, even if you were worried. Which is it, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I'd be worried at home and calm at work, because that's my job as a lead. My dad never let customers see him worried, even the year the shop nearly went under.

S2.say: I'd say we have to look after each other through families, churches and neighbours, because the government won't be ready. At the depot I'd say keep doing good work and don't panic, even if I was worried.
S2.think: It's frightening, because it's not just my job, it's Dev's too, and a pharmacy is the kind of place AI would take over quickly. We'd both be at risk just as we wanted to start a family.
S2.do: Puts off trying for a baby by about a year and cuts the trip to Dev's family abroad to build savings beyond four months. Asks the company to put her on training crews for the robots.
S2.feel: Anxious and scared, but with her family around her.
S2.quote: Telling her we're waiting because of robots would feel ridiculous, and also not ridiculous at all.
S2.fieldNote: The double risk to her and Dev makes this real, and the delayed baby is the sharpest cost. She leans on family and community before government. She openly owns the gap between a calm face at work and worry at home, modelled on her father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so let's not waste it. At the depot I'd say start learning the new tools as soon as they're proven. I'd say the same to the apprentices' families when they ask me if it's still worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is much better for us. We could still have the baby, and I'd have time to move into training the robot crews. Dev would have time to think about what pharmacists still do, probably the talking-to-people part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead with trying for a baby next year, as planned. I'd save more, maybe two hundred extra a month, and learn the AI and robot tools once the first crews have them. By year two I'd ask for a full training role, and do a short course in robot safety if the company offers one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's something to plan around, not something to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice's parents who ask if it's still worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them yes, finish the apprenticeship, because a trade teaches you how to work and how to be safe, and that's never wasted. But I'd also tell them to make sure their son or daughter learns the new tools. I wouldn't lie to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go ahead with the baby here, when you'd wait in the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in five years we'd have time to adjust, and the baby would be four by then, not a newborn. In two years, it would be a newborn and two lost jobs at the same time. That's too much.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so let's not waste it, and start learning the new tools once they're proven. I'd say the same to apprentices' families who ask if it's still worth it.
S3.think: Five years is much better for us: we could still have the baby and I'd have time to move into training robot crews. Dev would have time to think about what pharmacists still do.
S3.do: Goes ahead with trying for a baby next year and saves about two hundred extra a month. Learns the AI and robot tools once the first crews have them, and by year two asks for a full training role and a robot safety course.
S3.feel: Uneasy but okay, something to plan around rather than fear.
S3.quote: In two years, it would be a newborn and two lost jobs at the same time.
S3.fieldNote: The baby decision turns directly on warning time, and she explains it clearly. She sees training as her safe ground. She won't tell apprentices' parents comforting lies, which fits her direct style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people take responsibility for themselves and their families. At the depot I'd push for training the young ones for the jobs that will last. I wouldn't say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I feel fairly safe with ten years. We'd have our family started, Dev and I would both have time to adjust, and I'd be well into training by then. I'd be thirty-seven, and teaching is something I could do for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the baby as planned and maybe a second one later. I'd keep running the crew and training, and ask the company to move me fully into training within a few years. And I'd learn every new tool once it's proven, so I'm the one teaching it when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you less calm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company decided it didn't need trainers, because the robots train each other. I don't know if that's possible. If it is, I'd have to think again, but I'd have years to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own children to hear from you about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you do your work properly and you look after people, whatever the work is. My dad said that about the shop, and I say it to my apprentices. I don't think a robot changes that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people take responsibility for themselves and their families, and I'd push at the depot for training young ones for jobs that will last. I wouldn't say much online.
S4.think: I feel fairly safe with ten years: our family would be started, Dev and I would have time to adjust and I'd be well into training. At thirty-seven, teaching is something I could do for a long time.
S4.do: Has the baby as planned, maybe a second later, and keeps running the crew while training. Asks the company to move her fully into training within a few years and learns each new tool once proven.
S4.quote: That you do your work properly and you look after people, whatever the work is.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her faith in family, training and steady effort carries her through. Her only named risk is trainers themselves being replaced, which she admits she can't judge. Her values come straight from her father's shop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Dev and I would both be at risk just when we want to start a family, and two years isn't enough to change course. What would help is the companies paying for proper retraining, apprenticeships really, in the work that's left, and families and communities sticking together while it happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the women in the trade. It took a long time for women like me to get onto the poles. If the jobs shrink, I'd hate for us to be the first ones pushed out because we were the last ones in.

headlineQuote: I like seeing an apprentice go from scared of the pole to running up it, because I remember being that scared girl myself.
portrait: Hana Patel is a 27-year-old crew lead and apprentice trainer at the river town depot, and part of the storm team that travels after big storms. She's married to Dev, a pharmacist, they have about four months saved, and they hope to start a family next year. She learned from her parents' corner shop that you adapt rather than complain, and she uses AI now and then since Dev showed her. She's calm through the milder pictures, anxious about AGI in two years because both their jobs would be at risk and they'd delay a baby, and steadily calmer with more time, seeing training as her lasting role.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because both her and Dev's jobs would be at risk just as they want to start a family.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid retraining and apprenticeships in the work that's left, and families and communities sticking together through the change.
